extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent agents, patent examiners, inventors, and law students studying patent prosecution and litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and doctrinal standards governing caveats, abandonment (actual and constructive), continuity of applications, appeals, the nature and construction of letters patent, and related procedural and substantive patent-law principles used in drafting, prosecuting, and litigating patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory function of a caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: A caveat remains in force only one year; while in force its only statutory function is to prevent issuing any patent to another for the same invention until after the caveator has notice of the interfering application and thus an opportunity to file an application himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat's statutory role is preventive only — to delay issuance pending opportunity to file; it does not itself grant a patent or ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat as evidentiary proof of prior invention (completeness requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention is fully described in a caveat, then that caveat will constitute evidence showing that the invention was made at least as early as the caveat was filed; but this is incidental and cannot be performed by any caveat not complete enough in its description to enable a skillful mechanic, without inventing anything himself, to construct a specimen of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only a caveat sufficiently detailed to enable construction without further invention serves as strong evidence of priority; less-complete caveats only evidence the stage of development shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission to file or consider a caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission to file a caveat does not impair the ultimate rights of an inventor, and omission to consider a caveat does not invalidate a patent granted to another because of the oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to file/consider a caveat is not per se fatal to later rights; other remedies and doctrines may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of filing — wait for maturity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an immature invention is provisionally protected by a caveat or not, it should not be made the subject of an application for a patent until it reaches maturity; an immature- based patent may be too weak or narrow and may weaken later patents on matured inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic guidance: delay filing until the invention is sufficiently mature to support broad and valuable claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals from Patent Office decisions (procedural limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: No appeal lies from decisions of the Court of Appeals of the District of Columbia (on appeals from Commissioner of Patents) to the Supreme Court; but an appeal lies from decisions of any U.S. District Court or of the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia on bills in equity filed to compel issuance after unsuccessful appeals, to the appropriate Circuit Court of Appeals (or to the Court of Appeals of D.C. from the D.C. Supreme Court).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the available appellate routes in suits to compel issuance of patents following PTO rejections and administrative appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between actual and constructive abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for a patent may be abandoned actually or constructively; facts constituting actual abandonment of an application may also constitute actual abandonment of the invention, while constructive abandonment of an application may or may not work constructive abandonment of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat abandonment carefully — the legal consequences differ depending on whether abandonment is actual or constructive, and on surrounding facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity when withdrawn and refiled with intent
rubrics_metrics.description: If, when withdrawing an application, the applicant intended to file a new application for the same invention and accordingly does so, the two are held to constitute one continuous application for legal purposes (even if the new application is filed long after), provided there was no laches chargeable to the applicant on account of the delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent and absence of laches are key; continuity preserves priority and tolls relevant statutes when properly shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of statutory bars when applications are continuous
rubrics_metrics.description: When two applications are continuous the two years' public use or sale which may avoid the patent must be reckoned from the presentation of the first application, not from subsequent filings or amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity can preserve priority dates against statutory bars like the two-year public use/sale rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional application relation back
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an application covers two inventions and one is withdrawn by division and made the subject of a divisional application, that new application relates back to the original application and is not chargeable with any diminution of significance on account of the transaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a divisional preserves the filing date for the carved-out invention as to matters covered in the parent application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection + later prosecution does not necessarily abandon
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual abandonment does not necessarily follow from rejection and subsequent dormancy; if the applicant always expected to secure a patent and, without laches, made and prosecuted another application for the same invention and secured a patent, the two applications are considered one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court looks to applicant's intent and diligence; mere rejection followed by further prosecution, if timely and continuous, may preserve rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches defeats continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Laches intervening between a withdrawn or rejected application and a new application covering the same invention will be fatal to any claim of continuity and will constitute evidence that the first application was actually abandoned (and may evidence abandonment of the invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay attributable to applicant can forfeit claims to continuity and earlier priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawing one of two original applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an inventor makes two original applications and afterward withdraws one of them, he does not thereby abandon the invention described therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawal of one among multiple contemporaneous filings does not automatically constitute abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive abandonment — one-year incompleteness rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive abandonment of an application occurs whenever one year intervenes between the filing of the application and its being made complete enough to entitle it to examination under Patent Office rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must act to make applications complete for examination within one year or risk constructive abandonment unless condoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive abandonment — one-year inactivity after PTO action
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive abandonment also occurs if the applicant allows one year to pass without regularly prosecuting his application after any particular action is taken by the Patent Office and notified to him, unless the Commissioner is convinced the delay was unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to PTO actions promptly; the Commissioner may condone unavoidable delay but his decision is conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive abandonment — failure to pay final fee within six months
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive abandonment occurs when an applicant fails to pay the final fee within six months from the time a patent is allowed and notice of such allowance is sent to him or his agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely payment of allowance/final fees is mandatory to prevent abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution time compliance preserves application
rubrics_metrics.description: The period consumed by an applicant in prosecution of his application cannot be construed as abandonment of his invention or application, nor work to his prejudice provided he complies with Patent Office regulations on time limitations for taking actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow PTO rules on timing; compliant prosecution, even if lengthy, will not be treated as abandonment though it may affect litigation posture if art advanced during pendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive abandonment of application may cause constructive abandonment of invention (statutory-bar consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive abandonment of an application will work constructive abandonment of the invention covered thereby where the abandonment arose from causes stated (e.g., failure to make complete or prosecute) if no new application is filed soon enough to independently avoid the statute relevant to public use or sale more than two years before application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a new application promptly is required to avoid statutory bars; constructive abandonment may trigger public-use/sale statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive-abandonment cause that does not trigger public-use statute earlier
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive abandonment arising out of the cause stated in the last paragraph of §146 (presumably failure to pay final fee, etc.) will not put into operation the statute relevant to public use or sale more than two years before application; and probably will not activate other causes of constructive abandonment described in Section 104a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different types of constructive-abandonment triggers have different effects on when statutory bars start to run; some do not start the public-use clock earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory prerequisites for patent issuance (Commissioner's jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are authorized by law only on compliance with the statutory prerequisites to their issue; the Commissioner has no jurisdiction to grant a patent except where all those prerequisites have been substantially performed. If he inadvertently grants a patent otherwise, he exceeds his jurisdiction and any person sued for infringement may defend by pleading and proving the particular fault or omission with which the applicant was chargeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict compliance with statutory formalities/substantive prerequisites is required; an issued patent obtained in excess of jurisdiction is vulnerable as a defense in infringement suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy as alternative to patenting (limits and remedies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some inventors attempt to protect inventions by secrecy rather than patents; secrecy can be legitimate for certain processes or compositions but is seldom practical for machines/manufactures because assistance is needed; remedies for betrayal are contract damages or equity injunctions, but these are limited and ineffective against competitors who independently practice the betrayed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh feasibility of maintaining secrecy versus public patent protection; secrecy provides weak remedies against third-party independent use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents as property and constitutional protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent rights are property and the essence of the right is exclusion of others from its use; the owner is entitled to the same protection as owners of other property and cannot be deprived of that property without due process of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents enjoy strong constitutional protections; Congress cannot indirectly or directly destroy or seriously impair patent value except by eminent domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents are public franchises, not odious monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent are to be regarded not as monopolies created by executive authority but as public franchises granted to inventors of new and useful improvements to secure, for a limited time, their exclusive right as an incentive and compensation for reducing inventions to practice to promote the progress of useful arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy rationale for patents — balance of public benefit and inventor reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: State regulation of patent transfers (reasonableness principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: States may enact reasonable regulations (e.g., requiring filing authenticated copies of letters patent and affidavits when selling patent rights) as a protection against fraud; such statutes have been upheld where they are reasonable and not oppressive or inconsistent with federal statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State laws regulating patent transactions are permissible if they are reasonable safeguards and not in conflict with federal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity in descriptions and claims as conditions precedent to validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularity in descriptions and claims are conditions precedent to validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifications and claims must meet particularity requirements as a prerequisite for patent validity; be specific and particular in describing invention and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions of sufficiency of particularity are questions of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of sufficiency of particularity of descriptions and claims are questions of fact and not of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual inquiry (often jury or factfinder) determines whether particularity is sufficient; expect evidentiary presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to be construed in light of the descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are to be construed in the light of the descriptions (specification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting claim language, courts will read claims in context of the specification to ascertain the invention's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of claims in light of prior state of same art
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are construed in the light of the prior state of the same art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art context informs claim scope — claim language interpreted against what was known in the relevant art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of functional claims
rubrics_metrics.description: There are principles governing construction of functional claims (claims that define an invention by the function performed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional claim construction requires careful analysis (text references present but detailed guidance may be elsewhere in the chapter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic claims and specific claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between generic claims and specific claims (heading present).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice between generic (broad) and specific (narrow) claim drafting has strategic and validity implications; see chapter for elaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of inventions in a single letters patent / Double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues concerning plurality of inventions in a single letters patent and the doctrine of double patenting are recognized topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claiming multiple distinct inventions in a single patent and consider double-patenting rules when prosecuting continuations/divisionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper liberality and breadth of construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper liberality of construction and breadth of construction as governed by extent of use of the patent are principles for interpreting patent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should be reasonably liberal in construing claims but breadth will be limited by actual use, specification disclosure, and public notice considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction in light of application papers and contemporaneous statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims and letters patent may be construed in the light of application papers and contemporaneous statutes; questions of construction are generally questions of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prosecution history and contemporaneous statutory context as interpretive aids; ultimate claim construction is a legal determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters patent presumptions and notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent are presumed to be for the same invention as the application therefor; letters patent are constructive notice of their contents to every person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issued patents carry presumptions and give constructive notice; public is charged with knowledge of patent contents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation and other miscellaneous topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Other matters such as taxation of patents and territorial scope, operation on ships' decks, duration, beginning of term, to whom letters patent are granted, and letters patent as documents are listed as distinct subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These topics are recognized as separate doctrinal areas to be considered in patent practice; see full chapter for detailed rules.
